related_questions.question: How do I tell if I'm depressed?
related_questions.snippet: Feelings of sadness, tearfulness, emptiness or hopelessness. Angry outbursts, irritability or frustration, even over small matters. Loss of interest or pleasure in most or all normal activities, such as sex, hobbies or sports. Sleep disturbances, including insomnia or sleeping too much.
related_questions.title: Depression (major depressive disorder) - Symptoms and causes

text_blocks.snippet: Depression is a common and serious mood disorder that can affect how you think, feel, and handle daily activities. It's more than just feeling sad or irritable for a few days; it's a condition that can significantly impact various aspects of your life, including sleep, eating habits, and work. Depression is treatable, and early intervention is crucial for managing symptoms.
snippet_highlighted_words: a common and serious mood disorder that can affect how you think, feel, and handle daily activities

text_blocks.snippet: Here's a more detailed look at depression:

list.snippet: Persistent sadness or low mood: This is a core symptom, and it can last for extended periods.
Loss of interest or pleasure: Activities that were once enjoyable may no longer hold appeal.
Changes in appetite or weight: This can involve either significant weight loss or gain.
Sleep disturbances: Difficulty sleeping (insomnia) or sleeping too much (hypersomnia) are common.
Fatigue or low energy: Feeling tired all the time, even after adequate sleep.
Feelings of worthlessness or guilt: These can be intense and pervasive.
Difficulty concentrating or making decisions: Cognitive functions may be impaired.
Thoughts of death or suicide: In severe cases, these thoughts can be present.
Physical symptoms: Headaches, stomach problems, and other physical ailments can also occur.
Genetics: A family history of depression can increase the risk.
Brain chemistry: Imbalances in neurotransmitters like serotonin and dopamine may play a role.
Life events: Stressful events, such as the death of a loved one, financial problems, or relationship issues, can trigger depression.
Medical conditions: Certain illnesses, like chronic pain or diabetes, can contribute to depression.
Medications: Some medications can have depression as a side effect.

list.title: Medication:
list.snippet: Antidepressants can help regulate brain chemistry.

list.title: Psychotherapy:
list.snippet: Talking about your condition with a therapist can help you develop coping mechanisms and address negative thought patterns.

list.title: Electroconvulsive Therapy (ECT):
list.snippet: This is a more intensive treatment option, typically reserved for severe cases that haven't responded to other treatments.

list.title: Lifestyle changes:
list.snippet: Exercise, healthy diet, and adequate sleep can also play a role in managing symptoms.
If you experience symptoms of depression for most of the day, nearly every day, for at least two weeks, it's important to seek professional help.
If you or someone you know is having thoughts of suicide, call or text the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline or visit 988lifeline.org.

text_blocks.snippet: Important Note: Depression is a serious condition, but it is treatable. Early intervention and appropriate treatment can significantly improve the quality of life for individuals experiencing depression.
